title: Adidas shares rise after 'supershoe' helps seal sub-two hour marathon win
summary: STORY: Adidas shares rose on Monday (April 27) the day after a historic racing win.Investors bought in after Kenya's Sabastian Sawe became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours in an official race.He won the London Marathon wearing Adidas' Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3 trainers.Sawe finished the race in one hour 59 minutes and 30 seconds.The sub‑two‑hour marathon has been one of sport's biggest goals for years.Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha finished second in his marathon debut on Sunday.While Tigst Assefa broke her own women-only world record.All three were wearing the same make of Adidas trainers, which are due to go on sale on Thursday for a reported $500.The win is a boost for Adidas against arch-rival Nike.It comes after years of lab‑backed experiments and near‑misses looking to build a so-called "supershoe" to break the record.Nike's Breaking2 attempt at Monza in 2017 just fell short.Although Kenyan great Eliud Kipchoge ran under two hours in INEOS's 1:59 Challenge two years later.But those efforts fell outside the sport's official record books.Adidas said the Pro Evo 3 weighs an average 30% less than its predecessor and improves running economy by 1.6%.Adidas shares were up 2% in mid-morning trade, although they're down close to a fifth since the start of this year.That's due to concerns about the group's exposure to U.S. tariffs and the impact of the Middle East conflict.

title: Nike shares tumble after surprise sales drop forecast
summary: STORY: Nike shares tumbled in extended trade Tuesday, after it forecast a surprise drop in fourth-quarter sales. The sportswear giant blamed weakness in China and slow progress in clearing older inventory.That outlook sent its stock down more than 9%. Nike's revenue was flat at just under $11.3 billion in the third quarter, but just above analyst estimates.However, CFO Matt Friend projected a drop of up to 4% in current-quarter sales.Sales in China fell 10% and Friend said they are expected to fall 20% in the fourth quarter.He cited volatility from rising oil prices and ongoing fighting in the Middle East as factors.The company has struggled in its second-largest market, which accounts for 15% of annual sales.It has faced market share losses versus local competitors Anta and Li Ning.Nike is also expecting to end the fourth quarter with excess inventory.Under CEO Elliott Hill, it has pulled back promotions, stepped up innovation and refocused on core franchises like running.The move comes as the company works to reset the business after years of excess inventory and uneven demand across North America and China.

title: Sportswear brand On launches South Korea robot factory
summary: STORY: This factory in Busan, South Korea, is where sportswear brand On Running is using 32 robots to make its running shoes, in a push to speed up both manufacturing and delivery.The Swiss company said it's planning to open robot factories like this in the United States and Europe, too, as tariff hikes, supply chain disruptions and geopolitical risks are driving brands to manufacture their products closer to the end consumer.:: ROBOTS AT WORKIn a fierce competition with bigger rivals like Nike and Adidas to produce the fastest marathon running shoe, On has marketed its "LightSpray" shoe as a gamechanger for its lightness.The shoe is made with a robot arm spraying material onto a mold to create a sock-like design.COPPETTI: “The game changer will be making this product anywhere in the world close to consumer.”On's co-founder Caspar Coppetti says automation enables the brand to make shoes faster and closer to its key markets, and with less environmental impact.:: Caspar Coppetti, Co-founder, OnCOPPETTI: “I think the speed to market and the sustainability of it and also the fact that basically we're running out of places with cheap labor are all speaking for automation and get going closer to where consumers are.”According to its latest annual report, On currently sources 90% of its shoes from third-party manufacturers in Vietnam and 10% from Indonesia.On said planned robot factories in the U.S. would help lessen its tariff costs.COPPETTI: "I believe in free trade and so you know the more clarity we can get around tariffs and not having tariffs at all, I think will be beneficial for On.”Steep tariffs imposed by the U.S. on sportswear manufacturing hubs like Vietnam and China have weighed heavily on the industry over the past year, driving up production costs and squeezing margins.Now, the Supreme Court's ruling against tariffs has added fresh uncertainty, further clouding the outlook for retailers and importers.

summary: STORY: Nike on Tuesday reported a surprise rise in Q1 revenue and beat profit forecasts. The sportswear brand’s turnaround effort has gained traction…Despite weakness in China and U.S. tariff pressures. Also, the company’s wholesale revenues returned to growth and it managed to clear some of its bloated inventory. Signs of progress for CEO Elliott Hill’s plan to reinvigorate Nike. He’s vowed to refocus the brand around core sports like running, following a string of weak quartersHowever, executives warned the recovery was still a way off.Nike expects tariffs to cost about $1.5 billion this year - compared with the previously expected $1 billion. The sportswear brand makes nearly all its shoes in countries such as Vietnam that have been hit with steep duties under U.S. President Donald Trump.And China, Nike's third-largest market, has been a particular problem. Sales there fell for the fifth straight quarter for the three months ending August 31, as it faces strong competition from domestic brands.  Hill admitted Nike still had "work ahead to get all sports, geographies, and channels on a similar path."

title: Nike marketing plans in focus ahead of crucial year for sports events
summary: (Reuters) -Investors will zoom in on Nike's marketing plans for the coming year when it reports results on Tuesday, after several sluggish quarters in which rivals have stolen market share and high tariffs have hit imported goods.  The company, in the midst of a turnaround under CEO Elliott Hill, showed an appetite for big-ticket ad campaigns in the year ended May - boosting its marketing spend to $1.63 billion, up 9% from the previous year - and next year brings one of the biggest sports marketing bonanzas of the decade: the World Cup.  Marketing plans around the Cup, which will be held next June in the U.S., Canada and Mexico, will be a main investor focus in the coming months, Morningstar analyst David Swartz said.
